claims.text: A data-driven machine-learning model integrating existing experimental and simulation data can rapidly screen and predict optimal RHEA compositions.
Machine-learning-designed RHEAs can simultaneously achieve intrinsically high strength, improved ductility, and reduced weight.
The machine-learning approach will produce better-property alloys than traditional iterative thermokinetic and simulation-based design methods.
High-entropy alloys present a vast compositional design space.
RHEAs contain multiple principal refractory elements.
RHEAs have inherently complex microstructural features.
High-throughput computation can rapidly screen thousands of candidate HEA compositions.
Parallelized computational resources may be used to perform the proposed high-throughput screening.
Atomic-size differences, mixing enthalpies, and density-related parameters are key descriptors that the model must capture.
Tailoring alloy composition can alter lattice distortion and local atomic arrangements.
Lattice distortion and local atomic arrangements mediate dislocation mobility.
Changes in dislocation mobility can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
The same composition-mediated structural changes reduce overall alloy density.
A machine-learning model can identify compositional features correlated with severe local lattice distortion and favorable phase stability.
Severe local lattice distortion and favorable phase stability impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion results in improved mechanical performance and lower weight.
Traditional HEA design relies on iterative experiments and detailed thermokinetic or simulation-based analyses.
Model reliability depends on the quality and representativeness of the training data and may decline in unexplored compositional regimes.
Training-data bias and imperfect representation of complex microstructural phenomena create uncertainty in model predictions.
